newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - "Negative" spending flatters UK PSBR.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - "Negative" spending flatters UK PSBR.

text.p: Britain's public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) for 1996-97 will undershoot the official forecast by 3.0 billion stg, analysts say but the apparent improvement in the public finances is not all it seems.

Half of the undershoot comes from "negative" spending -- revenue from sales of fixed assets which is used to "cut" the amount of spending in the relevant department but not counted as privatisation proceeds.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) will publish the March PSBR data at 0830 GMT on Wednesday. Analysts expect a 1996-97 deficit of around 23.0 billion stg in the overall PSBR, compared with the official forecast of 26.4 billion and down from 31.7 billion in fiscal 1995-96.

Only assets sold in the form of shares are considered privatisation receipts. Straight sales, such as those of the armed forces married couples estate which has so far raised 0.9 billion stg, are merely negative spending.
Analysts say that this means that for the first time what is normally regarded as the core PSBR figure -- that excluding privatisation proceeds -- is actually distorted too.
The PSBR excluding privatisation proceeds is supposed to give a picture of what is really happening to the trend in government finances, without the effects of one-off boosts to revenue.
"That confusing of the issue is unhelpful. We should have a clear idea of what is a one-off and what is not," said Yamaichi chief economist John Shepperd.
"If we are adopting Southern European-style fudges, we should at least be up front about it," he said.
Excluding privatisation proceeds, analysts predict the deficit should come to 27.0 billion stg, compared with 34.1 billion stg in 1995-96.
But if the other fixed asset sales are also excluded, the 1996-97 deficit is actually likely to be 28.5 billion stg, a much less marked improvement.
The overall deficit for March itself is forecast at around 9.0 billion stg, up from 3.6 billion in February and 9.5 billion in March 1996.
Traditionally March prompts high spending as government departments try to ensure they have used up all their allocation so their funding is not cut the following year.
"The usual end of year surge in departmental spending is likely to be very much in evidence," said HSBC economist Jonathan Loynes.

But there will be revenue of 0.5 billion stg from the first instalment of the Housing Corporation loan book and of 0.1 billion stg in total proceeds from the sale of the Housing for Wales loan book which, as negative spending, will partially offset net departmental outlays.
The trend in the PSBR is still downward but analysts say that given the UK economy has experienced five years of growth, the level of government borrowing is unacceptably high.
"It's all very well saying we're heading towards balance -- we should be after five years in a steady recovery," HSBC's Loynes said.
"The problem is what happens if the economy starts to slowdown?"
